q: Which statements about ecology and evolution are true?
right: Ecology asks why organisms are distributed and abundant as they are
Genetic drift is a driver of evolution
Natural selection needs heredity
wrong: Ecology means 'study of life' in Greek
Extinction and local extirpation mean the same
Speciation requires gene flow between populations
why: oîkos = house. Extirpation is local; speciation needs reduced gene flow.

q: Which statements about niche and habitat are true?
right: The realized niche is shaped by competitors and predators
The fundamental niche is set by physiology and resources
wrong: Habitat and niche are synonyms
The realized niche is usually larger than the fundamental niche
A niche includes only abiotic conditions
Habitat is a species' role in the community
why: Habitat = where; niche = role and requirements, including biotic interactions.

q: Which statements about Darwin and Wallace are true?
right: Wallace's essay was sent from Ternate
Both were read at the Linnean Society in 1858
On the Origin of Species appeared in 1859
Wallace emphasised the environment as the force of selection
wrong: Darwin and Wallace agreed on human evolution
Darwin emphasised the environment, Wallace competition
why: Darwin: competition between individuals; Wallace: the environment.

q: Which ecogeographical rules are stated correctly?
right: Bergmann: larger bodies in colder climates
Allen: shorter extremities in cold regions
Gloger: darker pigmentation in warm, humid areas
wrong: Allen: larger bodies in colder climates
Gloger: lighter colours in warm, humid areas
Bergmann: longer ears in hot deserts
why: Bergmann = size, Allen = appendages, Gloger = colour.

q: Which statements about the island rule are true?
right: Small species tend to get bigger on islands
Large species tend to get smaller on islands
Relaxed predation is linked to insular dwarfism
Meta-analyses disagree on how general it is
wrong: All island species become dwarfs
It applies only to birds
why: Generally holds, but context- and lineage-dependent; methods matter.

q: Which traits describe a FAST life history?
right: Early maturation
Many small offspring
Short lifespan
High mortality
wrong: Few large offspring
Long lifespan
why: Fast: early, many, small, short-lived, high mortality.

q: Which statements match Group 1's conclusions?
right: Fast–slow is the dominant axis in tetrapods
Multiple axes are needed to describe all life-history variation
Altricial vs precocial offspring is an extra axis
wrong: Fast–slow fully explains invertebrate life histories
Life histories cannot be measured
Pace-of-life syndromes ignore behaviour
why: Stott et al. 2024: life histories are not just fast or slow.

q: Which statements about Allee effects are true?
right: A component Allee effect concerns one fitness component
A strong Allee effect has a critical threshold density
Below a strong-Allee threshold, per-capita growth is negative
wrong: A weak Allee effect always leads to extinction
A demographic Allee effect concerns only mate finding
Allee effects mean crowding always hurts
why: Weak: slower growth at low density, but recovery is possible.

q: Which are examples or mechanisms of Allee effects from Group 2?
right: African wild dogs: pup survival rises with pack size
Sea urchins: finding mates
Gypsy moth colonies below ≈107 males shrink
wrong: Snowshoe hares: fences keep out lynx
Lesser flamingos eating Spirulina
Bark beetles prefer cold climates
why: Mechanisms: mates, safety, teamwork, changing habitat.

q: Which statements about top-down and bottom-up control are true?
right: Top-down: consumers regulate lower trophic levels
Bottom-up: resource supply sets higher trophic levels
Trophic cascades alternate rises and falls in biomass
wrong: Bottom-up means predators control prey
Predation only covers kill-and-eat
Trophic cascades only move upwards
why: Predation includes parasitoids, parasitic castration, herbivory and seed predation.

q: Which results about snowshoe hares are correct?
right: Food plus predator exclusion gave the biggest effect
The decline was delayed, not prevented
Declines came mainly from lower survival before weaning
wrong: Food alone stopped the cycle
The cycle lasts about 2 years
Oli et al. used a fencing experiment
why: Krebs 1995: ~11× with both; Oli 2026: capture-mark-recapture over 43 years.

q: Which statements about food-web structure are true?
right: Degree is the number of links a species has
Modules interact more within than between clusters
Motifs are small link patterns that recur more than chance
Rewiring can be caused by species introductions
wrong: Keystone species are always the most abundant
Complex webs are always stable
why: Complexity supports resilience but is not automatically stable.

q: Which statements about the latitudinal diversity gradient are true?
right: Richness rises from the poles to the equator
Climate and energy are the main driver
Diversification is speciation minus extinction
wrong: Biotic factors are the main driver
Gradients are weaker in cold periods
Every taxon follows the gradient
why: Exceptions: parasites, aquatic flora, secondary marine mammals and birds.

q: Which pairings of diversity dimension and meaning are correct?
right: Functional: traits and ecological roles
Phylogenetic: evolutionary history represented
Taxonomic: number of species and evenness
Beta: difference between communities
wrong: Alpha: diversity across a whole region
Gamma: diversity at one sample point
why: Point → alpha → beta → gamma.

q: Which statements about counting species are true?
right: Mora et al. estimated about 8.7 million species
Cryptic diversity makes real diversity higher than taxonomy shows
Prokaryotic diversity is probably underestimated
wrong: The biological species concept works well for bacteria
Higher taxa have stopped growing
Different species concepts always give the same count
why: Over 700 new genera are described each year.

q: Which are species concepts named in the glossary?
right: Biological
Morphological
Phylogenetic
wrong: Ecological-energy
Latitudinal
Functional
why: Each highlights different processes and gives different counts.

q: Which of these are among the Big Five mass extinctions?
right: End-Ordovician
Late Devonian
End-Permian
End-Triassic
End-Cretaceous
wrong: End-Jurassic
why: Order: Ordovician, Devonian, Permian, Triassic, Cretaceous.

q: Which statements about the sixth mass extinction debate are true?
right: Ceballos defines mass extinction by rate
Wiens & Saban define it by total loss (75 %)
Extinction debt means losses already committed by past damage
wrong: Background rates come from the IUCN Red List
Total species loss today already exceeds 75 %
Extinction debt has no time lag
why: Background rates come from the fossil record (~2 E/MSY).

q: Which are DIRECT drivers of biodiversity loss?
right: Habitat conversion
Harvesting
Pollution
Species introductions
wrong: Population growth
Economic policy
why: Indirect drivers are social, economic, demographic, technological and institutional.

q: Which statements about Earth's biomass (Bar-On et al.) are true?
right: Plants make up most of the biomass
Livestock outweigh wild mammals
Biomass is measured in gigatons of carbon
wrong: Animals make up about half of all biomass
Wild birds outweigh humans
Wild mammal biomass has increased
why: Plants ≈450 Gt C; animals ≈2; wild mammals down ~82.5 %.

q: Which value statements are correctly labelled?
right: Intrinsic: nature has worth in itself
Instrumental: nature is useful for human needs
Relational: value from people's relationships with nature
wrong: Intrinsic: nature's market price
Relational: the dollar value of pollination
Instrumental: nature matters regardless of people
why: Instrumental = useful; relational = meaningful; intrinsic = regardless of us.

q: Which are regulating ecosystem services?
right: Climate regulation
Flood protection
Water purification
wrong: Timber
Outdoor recreation
Crops
why: Timber and crops are material; recreation is non-material.

q: Which statements about citizen-science data are true?
right: eBird records observation effort
Volunteer records are biased toward easy places and times
Occupancy–detection models can handle detection bias
GBIF aggregates occurrence records
wrong: Opportunistic data have a strict sampling design
Quality control happens before data collection
why: QA before/during, QC after.

q: Which statements about participation and principles are true?
right: Crowdsourcing is Haklay's Level 1
Extreme citizen science is Haklay's Level 4
ECSA wrote the Ten Principles
Participant feedback is one of the Ten Principles
wrong: Haklay's levels run from bad to good like Arnstein's ladder
Citizen science started with smartphones
why: The Christmas Bird Count dates from 1900.
